Your Excellency, Dr. Halil Rahman, President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Your Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, distinguished delegates, good afternoon. It is indeed a great honor and privilege to address this Assembly on behalf of Her Excellency, Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of the United Republic of Tanzania. Her Excellency, the President, asked me to convey her fraternal greetings and best wishes for the success of this session. Mr. President, allow me to congratulate you on your election to preside over the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Your immense experience and diplomatic skills give us confidence in your ability to guide the proceedings of this session successfully. Your election is also a fitting tribute to the great country, Bangladesh, with which Tanzania enjoys excellent relations. Mr. President, about 80 years ago, The United Nations was founded in San Francisco on a simple but enduring principle: that nations can prevent war and advance peace through trust, collective action, and respect the UN Charter. Today, war and insecurity are not only existential threats to our survival, but a range of challenges, including climate change, pandemics, un-governed artificial intelligence, and energy insecurity, just to mention a few. These challenges should remind us of a need for a stronger and much more coordinated United Nations. Therefore, the theme of this session, that is, restoring trust, Managing transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all, is timely for it requires us to revert to the founding principles of maintaining peace and restoring trust. Managing transformation requires reforming the UN to meet the realities of our time. In that regard, I commend our illustrious Secretary-General, His Excellency Antonio Guterres for championing the UN80 initiative that aims to advance the transformation agenda. In our opinion, the UN80 initiative must go beyond administrative efficiency to include overall organizational effectiveness, accountability, and representativeness for the United Nations to be able to deliver for all.

It requires us to unite our efforts to devise solutions that are capable of narrowing this gap by achieving just and comprehensive human-centered development and the right of every human to a dignified life. The theme of our session today reflects and accurately captures this noble goal. Better Together, 80 years and more for peace, development, and human rights. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen. The session is convened amidst a global context that is extremely complex and challenging. We see tensions, wars, conflicts that are escalating in various regions. We see also the exacerbating effects of terrorist threats and natural disasters resulting from climate change. Human suffering is increasing and the humanitarian burdens on entire populations are multiplying. This exposes international peace and stability to increasing risks and reinforces the need for a more effective role of the UN. Amidst all of this, the genocidal war being waged against our people in Gaza is a true litmus test to the human conscience and the credibility of the international system. We in the Islamic Republic of Mauritania condemn this aggression and this genocidal war and reiterate our support for the Palestinian people. And we stress that violence cannot bring lasting peace and security, and that stability in the Middle East as a whole depends inevitably on enabling the brotherly Palestinian people to realize their right to establish an independent state with East Jerusalem as its capital, in line with relevant international resolutions and the Arab Peace Initiative. In this context, we are pleased to have seen the momentum and the efforts to recognize the state of Palestine. That was powerfully demonstrated by the overwhelming vote in the UN General Assembly in favor of the New York Declaration on the implementation of the two-state solution, which was the outcome of the high-level international conference that was held in July 2025 at the initiative of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Republic of France.

“The world is changing. It is therefore up to us to take the appropriate decisions and orientations to make it better, for the well-being of our populations. Because the peace that we seek cannot be limited to a ceasefire, it ought to also help our country regain full control of its future by transforming the wealth that has too often gone to fuel conflict into tools for development and shared prosperity. Mr. President, It is another paradox that my country's experience is showing the world that some of its resources that fuel conflicts on its territory are also those that a growing proportion of a transformation of the global economy depend upon. The governance of strategic resources ought to be an issue of peace, development, and global security from now on. The energy transition, the electrification of transport, energy storage, as well as the expansion of digital and AI infrastructure are accelerating demand for copper, cobalt, lithium, nickel, and other critical minerals. As the largest global producer of cobalt and a major copper producing power, the DRC is at the heart of this transformation. Congolese cobalt is already being used in batteries, power grids, digital equipment, and technologies that are crucial for the decarbonization of the global economy. It would be both unjust and dangerous for added value, jobs, know-how, and technologies to remain concentrated far away from the communities that are making these changes possible. We cannot build a decarbonized economy through bloodstained minerals, and we will not bring about a just transition by reproducing a greenwashed version of our past dependencies. The DRC therefore rejects the old model that limits producer countries to crude extraction while processing, research, technology, and the bulk of the profits are concentrated elsewhere. Our ambition is clear. We no longer wish to be simply the basement of the world's economy. We plan to become a workshop, a laboratory, and a sovereign partner. We'd like to further transform cobalt and copper, process more cobalt and copper on our territory, develop precursors for batteries and industrial components, train our engineers, support our researchers, and include our enterprises in global value chains. We'd like to build together with our African and international partners, competitive regional businesses that create jobs, skills, and shared prosperity.

The issue of collective security that was the raison d’être of the United Nations has given way to uncertainty focused on other areas of human activity. His Majesty King Mohammed VI affirmed that in a message to the participants in the annual meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund, held in Marrakech, when he said,

This session is being held in a critical global context, marked by many challenges related to geopolitical tensions, climate change, poverty, migration, terrorism, hate speech, pandemics and natural disasters. Nevertheless, the current pace of scientific and technological progress may constitute a source of optimism, provided that the current challenges lead to international cooperation and solidarity in the promotion of scientific research, including artificial intelligence, and encourage sharing its benefits in strategic priority areas such as health security, energy transformation, food and water security, modern technologies and natural-disaster mitigation.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we must also prepare for the next great transformation, that of artificial intelligence, AI, which could become one of the greatest accelerators of human development. This is the prerequisite for AI to become not a new driver of divisions, but a tool for achieving emancipation, progress, and shared development. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, trust in international institutions is also linked to the trust people bestow upon their own institutions. For its part, Benin is continuing the process of consolidating our institutions and our democratic framework with full respect for our constitution and our legal order. We deem stability, public responsibility and citizen participation, we deem them essential preconditions for sustainable development. Our experience confirms our conviction: robust institutions, are one of the pillars of peace infrastructure. We stand convinced that while we might have different national trajectories, these trajectories should nevertheless converge towards the same end goal, giving all people the necessary conditions for them to be able to forge their future, living in peace, dignity, and stability. But we also have a very tragic, painful history, that of daughters and sons torn away from their land, separated from their families, and sent to different parts of the world, scattered. This history has left very deep wounds. It also, through generations, created a diaspora.

Madame President, this brings me to a question that is very dear to my heart. What kind of world do we want to bequeath to future generations? We often talk about young people as if they came from the future. Truth be told, they are already shaping the present. Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to ask ourselves if we're really preparing a future that is going to earn their trust. My personal experience has done nothing but reinforce this conviction. This year, I had the privilege of succeeding His Majesty King Carl Gustaf of Sweden as honorary chair of the World Scout Foundation. My longstanding commitment to the Scout movement has taught me a great deal about the power of intergenerational dialogue, solidarity, and the values of the Scout movement. also taught me something absolutely fundamental. Placing our trust in young people means giving them responsibilities, allowing them to take action. They're growing up in a world in which there are extraordinary possibilities, but it's also a world where uncertainty runs deep. Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are already transforming our way of life and the way in which we work. The enthusiasm they give rise to also goes hand in hand with the very real concerns. The current debates about the most extreme risks of AI remind us that technological progress cannot be divorced from responsibility. As we confront these transformations, we should endow our young people with the means to develop their critical thinking skills and their creativity. And this is exactly what education is supposed to do, transmit knowledge and competencies, but also to teach young people to call things into question, to open up to others and to shoulder your responsibilities. Against this backdrop, I believe that we should have one guiding principle. Human beings should be at the heart of all of our decision making. We must protect the rights, security and the well-being of all. We should also listen to young people, ask them what we can build working hand in hand.

We stand convinced that we need to build a better world in which we would live better together. We agreed on an ambitious program covering important issues such as peace and security, sustainable development, climate change, digital cooperation, in particular, ensuring that we make artificial intelligence, a technology that benefits all, in addition to human rights, gender equality, young people, future generations, and the transformation of global governance. Nonetheless, The aforementioned accomplishments cannot conceal the devastating consequences engendered by geopolitical and geo-economic fragmentation we're currently seeing. Conflicts are proliferating. They're dragging on in Ukraine, in Sudan, as well as in the Sahel. The unspeakable horror of what's going on in Gaza, where children are assassinated with impunity on a daily basis, where famine is being wielded as a weapon of war. while the international community is unable to effectively stop the genocide that's underway, as confirmed by the analysis report drafted by the United Nations and published on the 16th of September under the leadership of Judge Navi Pillay. The norms governing the use of force are being violated with chilling regularity. as illustrated by the bombing, the raids, and the extraterritorial assassinations committed by Israel. We condemn the terrorist attack against Qatar and the violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity. Speaking on behalf of the Republic, His Excellency Ismael Omar Kele, we reiterate our solidarity with the Emir, His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, as well as the government and the brother people of Qatar. The Security Council is paralyzed by the recourse to the veto, which has become systematic. International law and the norms which have guided us to date are being called into question, a dangerous trend. There's also a crisis of confidence between states, aggravated by the serious liquidity crisis owing to arrears in the payment of assessed contributions. Madam President, Secretary General, the Republic of Djibouti welcomes the recent adoption of the Severe Commitment, an outcome document at the... Financing for Development Conference, the fourth one.

The climate emergency demands action, development demands investment, and peace and humanitarian crises demand solidarity. The digital transition and artificial intelligence also offer new opportunities to accelerate development and improve the capacities of our states. Their potential, however, will only be fully realized if we are able to bridge the digital divide, facilitate technology sharing, and build the capacities of developing countries. And with that in mind, Djibouti supports the beyond GDP intergovernmental process. This seeks to complement traditional economic indicators with measures that better take into account people's well-being, social inclusion and environmental sustainability. Djibouti supports efforts to adapt the UN to contemporary challenges and enhance its effectiveness. But we must make it clear that our organization does not exist merely to balance the books. Rather, it is here to serve our peoples and to give effect to the decisions that we take together. Any reform should continue to be guided by the mandate established by Member States and should preserve the balance between the three pillars: peace and security, development and human rights. As the mandate of the outgoing Secretary-General, His Excellency Antonio Guterres, draws to a close, I should like on behalf of my president, His Excellency Ismael Omar Guelleh, to express our profound gratitude for his years of service to the UN. We wish him every success and we sincerely thank him for his invaluable contribution to global peace and justice. Finally, we are following very closely the process to identify the most qualified person to serve as the next Secretary-General of the UN. That selection must be guided by competence, professional integrity and unequivocal commitment to respect for international law and the ability rigorously to implement the reforms on which Member States have collectively agreed. Thank you.

We welcome the adoption of the Pact for the Future and its annexes, the Global Digital Compact and the Declaration on Future Generations (resolution 79/1). We live in an era of disruptive technological advances and complex challenges. Djibouti is grateful to the United States for having spearheaded the effort that led to the unanimous adoption by the General Assembly of resolution 78/311, the first-ever resolution on artificial intelligence, to promote safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development.

Given the world's unpredictable trajectory and the weakening of multilateralism, there is a pressing need, now more than ever, to restore the effectiveness of the United Nations on the basis of inclusive and equitable multilateralism. With this in mind, my country invites member states to reclaim the ideals enshrined in the UN Charter, as well as the constraints that fall to them as regards charter implementation. We call on member states to revive solidarity, solidarity which has always steered our actions. This is the collective commitment which will allow us, and of this I am certain, to tackle global challenges such as climate change, terrorism, scarce development financing, information wars, and regulation of artificial intelligence. Regarding the latter, a source of many hopes and fears, Cote d'Ivoire welcomes the adoption of the Pact for the Future and the annexes thereto, as well as the Global Digital Compact, regulating the use of artificial intelligence, AI. We call for the adoption of binding universal standards so as to regulate the use of AI and digital technologies to ensure that it is used to achieve development for the benefit of all. The UN's effectiveness during this critical period calls for, as a matter of priority, the completion of Security Council reform. The paralysis of this major organ consigns the United Nations and regional organizations to powerlessness. It pushes further away all prospects of peace and the lasting settlement of conflicts and the resolution of global challenges which threaten international peace and security. Now, more than ever, Security Council reform is vital for us to be able to adapt to new international realities and to strengthen the Security Council's legitimacy. Given the impasse which characterizes the negotiations process that's been underway for a number of decades, my country would like to reiterate its call for Security Council reform, which would, first and foremost, grant Africa its rightful place across all categories of this body, in keeping with the common African position expressed in the Izaruni Consensus and the Siut Declaration.

But two years after its adoption, negotiations on Security Council reform are still ongoing. The decision so urgently needed has yet to be made. The African position, represented for years now by the Ezulwini Consensus and the Cirt Declaration, is not a favor we're asking. It is a demand for justice and effectiveness. Transformation next requires peacekeeping operations with realistic mandates and predictable financing. We support strengthening the UN-African Union partnership, including through predictable financing for African-led operations. Lastly, the transformation requires an international financial architecture that stops penalizing fragile countries. These reforms are not favors. They are investments in the world's stability. The UN must benefit all of its members. Mr. President, digital transformation and the rise of artificial intelligence are rightly considered to be one of the great promises of our time. The Global Digital Compact must become a reality. Affordable connectivity, skills transfer, data protection, and a governance of AI in which developing countries decide instead of simply being users. The transformation also requires facing history with lucidity. The wounds left behind by colonization are still being felt on our continent. Reparations are not simply reopening a feud of the past. They are a demand for justice for the future, recognition of the wrongs committed, restitution of cultural goods and archives, equitable cooperation, debt relief. There are many possible paths. The African Union has prioritized this, and the CEAR fully supports these efforts. Transformation calls for real respect for the sovereignty of states. Sanctions and restrictions must be tools for peace and must be adjusted in accordance with the progress made. They must not be retaliatory measures serving geopolitical interests. Mr. President, we are at a crossroads. We have our diagnoses. It is now time for decision. That is why the CAR calls upon the UN to act. Saving the world is not a task for one nation or one continent. It is our collective will to action that this 81st session be one in which we stop taking stock and begin taking action. Thank you for your kind attention.

worsening inequality, debt levels which are reducing the room for maneuver available to many states, as well as climate upheaval, which is hitting the most vulnerable the hardest. At the same time, we're witnessing technological transformation on a vast scale. It's accelerating. AI is already transforming knowledge, work, our economies, education and information. Never has humanity had so many different means to shape its fate. However, nor has humanity ever been so acutely aware of the need to make collective decisions about how these means should be used to serve the common good. This is why the theme of this 81st session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a UN that delivers for all, resonates so strongly. The true challenge of our time is not just managing a succession of crises, but it is restoring our collective capacity to anticipate, to make decisions, to act. before these crises become irreversible. Mr. President, Benin believes in multilateralism. We believe not because we harbor nostalgia for the world of 1945, but because in 2026, the world more than ever needs a forum where states can talk to one another, listen to one another, and act in concert. Defending multilateralism also means taking a lucid look at the United Nations Organization. Trust, indeed, is not something you can order. It takes shape when our organization can respond to the expectations of our people, the people it serves, when the organization can deliver concrete results. It is in this spirit that Benin supports the efforts undertaken within the framework of the UN80 initiative. We need to achieve greater efficiency, coherence, transparency and responsibility. Nonetheless, we should remain cognizant of a key requirement. Reforming the UN doesn't simply mean cutting costs. What it should mean is boosting the organization's impact. A more effective United Nations should be better positioned to prevent conflicts, to respond to humanitarian crises, to shore up development, and anticipate the transformations which are already shaping our future. It should also remain true to the principles which underpin its legitimacy, universality, the sovereign equality of states, solidarity, and respect for the UN Charter.

The challenge now lies in our collective ability to mobilize them and to channel them with greater equity, solidarity, and effectiveness in the service of sustainable development. Cote d'Ivoire therefore calls for an ambitious reform of the international financial architecture and a renewed global partnership. to ensure that developing countries have more equitable access to the resources needed to finance infrastructure, health, education, energy, industrial transformation, and the creation of decent jobs for young people. Climate challenges require a similar degree of mobilization. Africa contributes the least to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains among the regions most hit the hardest by their consequences. Droughts, floods, land degradation, and the disruption of food systems directly threaten the ways of life and the livelihoods of millions of people. In this context, honouring international commitments on climate finance, adaptation and technology transfer is an imperative of justice and solidarity. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the transformation that our world is experiencing is also a technological one. Artificial intelligence and the digital revolution are opening up considering opportunities in many areas of our contemporary world. However, these technological advances can also exacerbate existing divides if their development as well as access to them remain unevenly distributed. In this regard, Cote d'Ivoire supports the efforts of the United Nations to promote the global governance of artificial intelligence that fosters innovation while protecting human dignity, international security, and sustainable development in a spirit of inclusion, ethics, and equitable sharing of the benefits of technological progress. Mr. President, the trust that we seek at the international level must also be built within each of our states. through the strength of our institutions and our ability to create the conditions for sustainable and shared development. My country, for its part, under the leadership of President Alassane Ouattara, continues on its path towards a stronger and more diversified economy while taking care to ensure and safeguard peace and stability.

Hence, we call for a reform of its bodies, starting with its Security Council, this so as to make these bodies more representative, more transparent, and closer to the realities of our world. One can see clearly that the Security Council in its current composition no longer reflects the geopolitical balance of our world. Thus, the urgent need to reform it not in theory, but in practice. Africa cannot remain marginalized. This is a continent with more than 1,400,000,000 residents. It is a continent of the future, of the youth, of potential, for which today we need to ensure full and complete participation in global decision making. I wish to state forcefully, Africa deserves permanent representation on the United Nations Security Council, not as the beneficiary of a favor, but as a legitimate partner. This is the solemn call that the Republic of the Congo wishes to sound from this high rostrum. We must invent a smarter multilateralism, a more effective multilateralism, one that is closer to the aspirations of the people, and one that is more representative of the realities of the 21st century. This multilateralism also needs to be made manifest through concrete acts, through tangible results, and through sustainable solutions. The peoples of the world will not judge us by our speech, but rather by what we succeed in accomplishing together. Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, there can be no lasting peace without development, and the opposite is true as well. Poverty, inequality, youth unemployment, exclusion, This is the ground that produces frustration, instability, and violent extremism. We must honor our commitments for the financing of the Sustainable Development Goals and put an end to the machinery that strangles vulnerable economies. such as unsustainable debt or unfair trade rules. International solidarity remains vital to allow for developing countries to successfully weather their transition toward a more prosperous future. This is the reason why we need to invest massively in education, in health, agriculture, infrastructure, new technologies, artificial intelligence, inter alia. The climate is a very big challenge today. It goes beyond all borders, beyond all divisions.

We propose also the establishment of a global charter for digital governance and ethical artificial intelligence so that human rights are protected in the digital sphere. We call on the establishment of a global index of equity and democratic resilience in addition to GDP to measure dignity, to measure justice and inclusion. My country is already acting within its means. We have validated our third national report on Resolution 1325, Women, Peace, and Security. We have updated our follow-up plan of Beijing plus 30. We're strengthening national accountability mechanisms to put women, young people, and the most vulnerable at the heart of public policies. On this 80th anniversary of the UN, let us recall the vision of its founders to substitute the force of the powerful by the force of law and to build a future of dignity for all. Thank you very much.

In addition to facing security and climate challenges, the world is being shaped by a technological revolution for which few countries are prepared. Artificial intelligence holds great promise for our societies, but it can also pose a number of threats and lead to abuses, owing to the lack of international regulations governing its use. Consequently, it is incumbent upon us to ensure that that revolution does not exacerbate inequalities or lead to the digital disadvantage of part of humankind, but that, on the contrary, it promotes the progress and well-being of all. It is for that reason that my country welcomes the adoption of the Global Digital Compact (see resolution 79/1), which should enable better use of that technological advance, in the service of the progress of all nations.

We reiterate the fact that we are available to accompany our brotherly countries in their work to achieve return to peace and stability. Through our history, we know that peace is difficult to build, but it is the only victory that benefits one and all. Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies. guided by the same sense of responsibility. The recurring Ebola outbreaks and repeated pandemics have shown that global threats are no longer solely military or economic. Health security has become an essential component of collective security. And here, we will continue supporting the strengthening of the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville and will shoulder all of its responsibilities in accordance with the 1952 Headquarters Agreement. We also call for international governance of artificial intelligence in outer space. These technologies must remain in the service of humanity, progress, and the empowerment of peoples. Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination. Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation, and digital sovereignty. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to conclude, the Republic of the Congo remains faithful to its principles, peace, development, sovereignty, good neighborliness, dialogue, cooperation, and mutual respect amongst nations. We will continue to defend our national interests while fulfilling our international responsibilities. We will continue to believe in Africa and in our shared destiny, and we will continue to choose the United Nations as a privileged space for dialogue amongst people. I thank you.

Access to information in a universal, equitable and financially affordable manner, as well as to the instruments providing access to it, is also one of the major challenges of modern times. The Internet claims to represent a relationship of rapprochement between spaces and peoples, but the so-called spider web favours rich countries while developing countries are still poorly connected, particularly in Africa. At a time when the world and trade are becoming increasingly digital, it is becoming imperative for all countries to have access to the Internet, including artificial intelligence, which is revolutionizing the world as we speak. The increasingly widening and gaping abyss between the countries of the global North and the global South is causing the latter to lose a large number of social, scientific and economic opportunities. As leaving no one behind is one of the pillars of United Nations action, it is more than urgent that the digital divide be bridged in the legitimate interest of current and future generations.

Through FID alone, we are increasing domestic food production and strengthening food security. Through free quality education, we are widening the path for the circumstances of a child's birth, from a child's birth to the future that awaits that child. In 2024, we enacted the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act and subsequently championed the proclamation of 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. A girl in Sierra Leone is no more or less precious than a girl anywhere else in our beautiful world. Protecting her childhood education and freedom as part of what development is supposed to mean. A gas future, like the future of every young person, will be shaped by forces already remaking our world, climate change, artificial intelligence, and the energy transition. The meaning of for all becomes more urgent as we decide how these transformations will be governed. Artificial intelligence can improve, of course, education, health, agriculture, and public administration. It can also widen the inequality if infrastructure, knowledge, and rule-making remains concentrated in a few countries. Developing nations must help shape the standards that will govern technologies affecting their people. Climate change presents the same moral question in harsher form. Who benefits? Who decides? And who pays? In Shenge on Sierra Leone's southern coast, families watch the sea take their land, fishing grounds, and the graves of their ancestors. For them, climate change is the disappearance of home in the present. Those who contributed least to the climate crisis are bearing some of its gravest, greatest cost. Accessible and predictable climate finance, support for adaptation, and effective arrangement for loss and damage are obligations of justice. They are also investment in global stability Fairness in transformation depends on the institutions that govern it. Sierra Leone, therefore, supports the UNH initiative and wider reforms that make this organization more effective, accountable, and responsive. Efficiency matters, and reform must preserve the capacity to act. Mr. President, The choice of the next Secretary-General offers another test of institutional effectiveness and equality. In 80 years, every Secretary-General has been a man.

With the adoption of the Pact for the Future (resolution 79/1), including the Declaration on Future Generations and the Global Digital Compact, at the Summit of The Future, my Government is reinforcing its commitment to championing and investing in human capital development. Human capital development is a profound commitment to our people’s well-being and future. By investing significantly in education, healthcare and agriculture, my Government is laying the foundation for a prosperous and equitable Sierra Leone. Over the past six years, our achievements through our Free Quality School Education Programme, legislative reviews, governance reforms in the education sector and radical inclusion strategy have been highly impactful, well acclaimed and seen as a good model for the world. We welcome the Global Digital Compact’s principle of ensuring safe, secure and trustworthy emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to offer new opportunities to accelerate development, leaving no one behind.

But we urge that our national ambition be supported by international action to make climate finance accessible, predictable, and adequate, including through the sustained implementation of the new collective quantified goal on climate finance and effective management to address loss and damage, build climate resilience, and a fairer international order in which those who have contributed least to the climate crisis are not left to bear the greatest burdens. Mr. President, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but opportunity without inclusion can become another source of inequality. The digital divide must not become the next development divide. Developing countries must not remain passive consumers of technologies designed elsewhere. We need the capacity to participate in research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and global technology governance. Technology must serve humanity, and the governance of artificial intelligence must be inclusive responsible, and grounded international cooperation. This is particularly important for the world's least developed countries. As the Gambia prepares to assume greater leadership within the Global Coordination Bureau of the LDC group, we do so with a clear sense of responsibility. LDCs continue to face structural constraints, including limited productive capacity, high debt burdens, climate vulnerability, narrow export base, technological gaps, and restricted access to affordable finance. We will continue to advocate for full implementation of the Doha Program of Action. Mr. President, migration is another area where our collective response must be guided by human dignity and shared responsibility. Migration continues significantly to economic development, cultural exchange, and human progress. Yet, irregular migration continues to expose young people and vulnerable populations to exploitation, trafficking, abuse, and tragic loss of life. We must strengthen cooperation for safe, orderly, and regular migration, protect the rights and dignity of migrants, and expand lawful pathways for labor mobility, as well as invest in young people, women, education, health, and social protection to safeguard sustainable development and lasting peace. Mr. President, The government welcomes the call for the reform of United Nations. We recognize the constraints facing the organization was limited with limited resources and increasing demands.

My country also harbors 42% of the remaining Upper Guinea rainforest, a vital global carbon sink that we maintain on behalf of all humanity. Climate responsibility must be paired with climate justice. We call on industrial nations to honor their financial pledges and operationalize loss and damage mechanisms. Democracy and human rights and responsible innovation. Mr. President, the ultimate measure of governance is inclusion. In Africa, 60% of our population is under 25. the single greatest engine of innovation on earth. We must equip our youth with STEM education, digital literacy, and technical training so they become co-creators in the global digital economy, not just consumers. Gender equality remains essential When women lead, peace agreements last longer, economies grow faster, and governance becomes more accountable. Liberia remains committed to full political, economic, and social equality for women and girls. Liberia welcomes global effort to govern new technologies including the Secretary General's independent international scientific panel on artificial intelligence. Developing nations must not be left behind as mere consumers or algorithms designed elsewhere. We must be supported in building true digital sovereignty. We join calls abiding ethical norms and greater regulation of artificial intelligence, particularly in warfare. Innovation must protect human development, not automate human destruction. Reforming global governance, correcting historic injustice. Mr. President, 80 years of patience is enough. The time for structural reform is now. While we welcome the UN80 reform agenda to make this organization agile, efficient, and accountable, true reform must address the core structural issue. The UN Security Council article is home to 1.5 billion people and account for nearly one third of the UN membership. Yet 80% of Security Council mandates concern Africa peace and security, while Africa remains without a single permanent seat on the organ responsible for global peace. This historical injustice is no longer tenable. Liberia reaffirms its support for common African position and proposed reform of the United Nations Security Council. We celebrate the presentation of the African model during the recent intergovernmental negotiation which advances us towards text-based negotiation.

Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but also serious risks of exclusion, manipulation of the society, and even militarization throughout autonomous weapons. These advances pose new challenges to the defense and human dignity, justice, and labor. As long as we do not fully understand how these models work, we cannot entrust them critical tasks without robust safeguards in place. Otherwise, we are going to destroy the world. For that reason, Mozambique advocates a technological and climate diplomacy capable of regulating risk and democratizing benefits. through genuine transfer and sharing of knowledge, of technology, so that the science and technology are not factors of exclusion, but rather instruments of climate justice and inclusive development in the world. Faced with these interconnected challenges, our continent, Africa, can and must play an active role in defining international roles and standards, formulating principles and scientific ethics, and determining research priorities, ensuring that technology innovation is always at the service of the humanity and not the service of destruction of the humanity. In face of this crisis, the isolation is not the answer. Constructive dialogue and strengthening of multilateralism are. The Pact for the Future, adopted in 2024, offers concrete and innovative responses for relaunching of multilateralism adapted to challenges to the 21st century. Mozambique, as an African country with vast natural resources and unparalleled cultural wealth, has distinguished itself in the promotion and strengthening of democracy in the African continent. Since we moved forward with political pluralism, we've been working tirelessly to consolidate the foundation of a robust democratic system, holding regular and transparent elections that reflect the will of people and ensure that every Mozambican citizen has the voice and a say in the decisions that shape the future of our nation in Mozambique. Indeed, our presence in this podium is a result of a free and a transparent process of the Mozambican people from Rovuma to Maputo, from Zumbo to Indico, and in the diaspora. We have historically had an ongoing commitment to dialogue and building bridges between different political and social actors.

that resilience is now an environmental, economic, and food security, social for development issue, and increasingly one of peace and security in all the world. We therefore reiterate the need to increase funding for adaptation, facilitate access to climate funds, operationalize the loss and damage mechanisms, and invest in early warning systems and resilient infrastructure. Mozambique remains highly vulnerable to extreme weather events, floods, inundations, cyclones, and we are concerned with the El Nino that might have potential severe impact in the central and southern parts of the country, especially when it comes to drought, food insecurity and livelihood. The preparedness and international cooperation will be essential to mitigate these impacts in a context where humanitarian needs are already facing a severe funding shortfall in the whole world. Mr. President, digital transformation remains or demands the same solidarity that we are talking about because Africa must not limit itself to supplying the minerals that fuels the world innovation hubs. We need to have investment in connectivity, computing capacity, scientific research, training of young people in Africa, technology transfer, governance, ethics for AI in the spirit of partnership that builds capacity and promotes autonomy of our sovereignty states. Thus, Mozambique reiterate its support for the objectives of the UN aid initiative to make this organization more effective, coherent, inclusive, representative and suited to the challenges of our time. Reform must be embraced as political commitment focused on concrete results. Reforms must also correct imbalances in representation of global governance. In this regard, Africa cannot continue to be in a center of the Security Council agenda while remaining absent from its rank of permanent members. Africa must be a permanent member of the Security Council of the UN. We therefore reaffirm the common African position related to the reform of the United Nations Security Council based on the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, under which no fewer than two permanent seats with all prerogatives and privileges, including the veto, as long as it exists, and five non-permanent seats are allocated to Africa.

Namibia acknowledges the technological advance in all fields, but ethical boundaries must be respected. However, artificial intelligence must not be a substitute for human judgment or responsibility. We therefore call for a global standard that ensure that the usage of artificial intelligence remain transparent, fair for humanity. Youth unemployment, increased economic inequality, lack of adequate housing, quality education and healthcare, water, energy and debt distress are among the common challenges that no one country can address alone. Through multilateral cooperation, our collective action must ensure that we all forge ahead to make the world a better place and to work together on those challenges in line with our theme, "Better Together." Madam President, 30 years since the adoption of the Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action, we have much to celebrate and to ponder on. Namibia continues to make progress in the area of women participation in politics and decision-making. Currently, Namibia's cabinet has 57% of women. As we gear up to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on women, peace, and security, adopted during Namibia's presidency of the UN Security Council, Namibia will host two high-level events in Windhoek and New York. I look forward to the participation of all Member States in those events to collectively reaffirm commitment to the Women, Peace and Security agenda. And through the Namibia International Women Peace Centre, we will continue to advocate for the universal implementation of the Women, Peace and Security agenda. Madam President, we know to the ongoing efforts of the UN to ensure that we remain fit for purpose, including the UN8 initiative. We need an agile United Nations that is inclusive. Respect of the UN Charter and its purpose and principles must be our guiding star for our future endeavors. Madam President, we are meeting against a backdrop of profound global tension. The world is fractured by conflict, displacement, and economic instabilities, straining multilateral cooperation and a serious issue for us to reach consensus, a global liquidity crises threaten to plunge millions of people into poverty and insecurity.

While the pact gives due consideration for the interest and the needs of the future generation, its implementation has not been as effective as we had wished. For Namibia, effective implementation of the key commitment of the Pact for the Future would be beneficial in accomplishing Namibia's national priorities, namely agriculture, sports, youth empowerment, quality education and training, creative industry, health and social welfare, land, housing, and sanitation. I wish to urge all member states to consider the implementation of the Pact for the Future as a crucial international priority for development. As part of our developmental agenda, we are preparing our young people for the emerging industries in Namibia, such as oil and gas, renewable energy, and green hydrogen, among others. Subsequently, this year we have introduced 100% subsidised registration and tuition fees for Namibian students entering universities and vocational training centres and encourage them to take up appropriate courses. The Government of Namibia has established the National Youth Development Fund last year. As a result of this fund, young people have set up their own medical practice, law firms milling plants, pottery business, to mention a few, thus contributing to job creation and poverty eradication. Namibia also takes cognizance of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence in advancing human progress in line with the Global Digital Compact. However, We call for ethical, responsible, inclusive, and human-centered development and use of artificial intelligence with appropriate safeguard to ensure that technological advancement complements and enhance human capability rather than undermine it. A United Nations that delivers for all must be inclusive. I reaffirm Namibia's unwavering solidarity with the people denied their right to self-determination. This position is firmly rooted in Namibia's historical experience of the brutality and colonialism apartheid and occupation.

Global action on disaster resilience and predictable financing for a just energy transition is essential if international cooperation is to deliver for all. Our continent has the world's largest reserves of critical minerals. These critical minerals can help bridge the gap between wealth and poor nations and overcome the indignities of poverty and underdevelopment. We insist, Mr. President, that indeed, Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and the deployment of artificial intelligence. We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source of critical minerals and research and innovations for artificial intelligence. Restoring trust in multilateralism demands that we demonstrate, as the United Nations, that peaceful resolutions of conflicts is still our mantra. Unfortunately, much of what we see runs counter to this. In the last two years, the world spent more on military budgets than on resourcing this important body tasked with maintaining global peace. We are reminded that meeting the SDGs by 2030, including ending hunger and expanding access to safe water and sanitation, will require not more than 5% of the 2.9 trillion US dollars spent on arms. The results of the choice we are making is an arms race and the world as divided as it is dangerous. We see the consequences in Sudan, which is today the worst humanitarian crisis in the world. We see also the consequences in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, in Iran, Ukraine, and elsewhere, humanitarian workers are caught in the crossfires of today's conflict. When they are not being obstructed from reaching civilians in need, they are being killed in the line of duty. To restore respect for international law, we must protect those who deliver humanitarian assistance. That is why South Africa endorses the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, supported by nearly 120 states, from all regions of the world. Mr. President, 80 years ago, the first resolution of the General Assembly called for the elimination of nuclear weapons.

In this regard, Botswana reaffirms its support for comprehensive Security Council reform and aligns itself with a common African position as articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration. We believe that a Security Council that continues to exclude Africa and Latin America from permanent membership cannot credibly claim to reflect contemporary geopolitical realities. We also call on the United Nations to continue to explore the creation of an inclusive international framework on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. We recognize technology as a bridge that narrows global inequality. This extends to critical minerals, rare earths, and energy resources that power the technological revolution, many of which come from developing countries. Therefore, Developing countries must have a meaningful voice in setting the standards and safeguards that will govern these technologies, ensuring that they expand opportunities, support decent work, and strengthen public services while protecting human dignity, rights, and security. Mr. President, I wish to reaffirm Botswana's commitment to multilateralism. We believe that shared challenges require shared solutions. We also believe that implementing the Pact for the Future, together with the UN80 initiative, offers an opportunity to translate our shared commitments into practical improvements in the functioning of the United Nations. In conclusion, Mr. President, I reemphasize that restoring trust Managing transformation and delivering for all are interconnected. We restore trust when we uphold our commitments, respect the UN Charter, and apply international law consistently. We manage transformation when change creates opportunity rather than deepens inequality, when developing countries have a meaningful voice in shaping the system that affect their future. And when technological and economic progress serve humanity as a whole. And we deliver for all when our decisions translate into tangible improvements in peace, security, development, health, and human dignity. The difference our decisions make in the lives and livelihoods of people is the standard against which the credibility of the United Nations must be measured. Botswana is ready to work with all member states. We may be small in size, but we are sturdy in principle.

The Republic of Malawi is optimistic that AI will usher in a new era of enhanced productivity for its citizens, helping to propel the country's development trajectory. Madam President, let me take this opportunity to express my gratitude to your office for convening a high-level plenary meeting to commemorate the 30th anniversary of the World Programme of Action for Youth. The youth make up a large proportion of the population of Malawi and, indeed, in Africa. They are an indispensable force for sustainable development. They are leaders, major actors and beneficiaries of investments and creators of wealth for today and tomorrow. It is for this reason that the government of Malawi developed the 2023-2028 National Youth Policy to demonstrate its commitment to place young people at the center of the national development agenda and to undertake reforms which support effective engagement of youth in policy development, implementation, and monitoring in all sectors. Two notable areas that the Republic of Malawi has proudly championed in relation to youth and development is the youth peace and security agenda and youth innovation and entrepreneurship. To that end, we are investing in education, vocational training, and meaningful political and economic participation of our youth. We have an inclusive national peace architecture that enables women and youth to participate as negotiators, mediators and community leaders. We have also created a Youth Innovation Fund that supports youth innovators and entrepreneurs to realize their dreams. We therefore urge the international community to create concrete pathways for youth inclusion in political and economic decision-making processes. Let us invest in their potential, not just fear their energy. To that end, the Republic of Malawi calls for investing for peace through a dedicated funding for youth-led peacebuilding. Madam President, in closing, the Republic of Malawi reaffirms its unwavering commitment to multilateralism and to the central role of the United Nations in addressing the pressing challenges of our time. But let us be clear. Noble mandates alone will not deliver results unless they are matched by the necessary resources, fairly allocated and predictably provided.

We therefore call for increased investment in early warning systems, climate-smart agriculture, and social safety nets. A world that is food secure is a world more peaceful. Considering these challenges, Madam President, the Republic of Malawi urgently calls for bold and accelerated climate action that includes the full and effective implementation of the Paris Agreement. This involves not only enhanced commitments to reduce emissions, but also significant scaling up of financial resources dedicated to climate adaptation, addressing loss and damage, and ensuring equitable access to sustainable technologies. The Republic of Malawi firmly believes that only through a collective sense of responsibility and international solidarity can we protect our planet and provide a sustainable future for our generations to come. Beyond various agreements and boardroom meetings, time for action is now. We must act decisively to safeguard both our environment and the livelihoods of those most at risk. Madam President, the global community also needs to work together to address public health issues. My delegation, therefore, applauds your office for the efforts that led to the adoption of the Political Declaration on the Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases and the Promotion of Mental Health and Well-Being. No nation has been spared from the impact of these two health issues, whose causes are numerous. The response to these issues requires concerted efforts and collaboration. It is, therefore, rather disheartening that the political declaration faced many hurdles during the negotiation process. My delegation wishes to appeal for shared commitment to address the issues and, indeed, all other emerging public health issues. Madam President, In this digital age, artificial intelligence presents both unprecedented opportunities and profound challenges. If harnessed responsibly, AI can accelerate development, improve health and education, and unlock economic growth. Yet, without clear governance, it risks deepening inequalities and undermining security. We therefore call for a global framework that ensures AI is ethical, inclusive, and accessible to all nations, enabling it to serve as a force for development rather than division.

By producing essential medicine within Africa, the entire world gained through stronger health security and stable supply chains, especially through faster outbreak response. Mr. President, the fifth opportunity is to promote human rights, peace, and international security. Malawi firmly believes that development, peace and human rights are inextricably linked. We remain deeply committed to upholding the constitutional rights of all our citizens, strengthening our democratic institutions and maintaining an uncompromising stance against corruption. Furthermore, we strongly defend the right to development as an inalienable human right. True freedom cannot exist in condition of extreme poverty and systemic economic exclusion. On the global stage, we view with great alarm the proliferation of violent conflicts and constitutional changes of government, geopolitical fragmentation, and acts of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Mr. President, the Malawi nation is not standing alone. As all these alarming developments occur, Malawi continues to play its part in global peace operations, deploying our brave men and women to United Nations peacekeeping missions to safeguard stability on our continent. In this regard, let me reiterate the call for immediate cessation of hostilities in all active conflict zones worldwide. Global resources currently being funneled into destructive warfare should instead be redirected towards eradicating poverty, building schools and financing sustainable development. We also reaffirm our solidarity with global efforts to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. Mr. President, as we take steps to grab these opportunities, we must also recognize the emergence of artificial intelligence, which presents both opportunities and threats to humanity. Malawi welcomes the transformative potential for AI as an expression of human ingenuity and as an increasingly important tool for accelerating sustainable development. For developing countries, including Malawi, AI offers opportunities to strengthen agricultural productivity and food security, improve healthcare and education, enhance climate resilience and disaster preparedness, expand financial inclusion, and improve the efficiency of public service. Malawi believes, however, that technological advancements must remain human-centered. Artificial intelligence should complement and enhance human capabilities rather than diminish the indispensable role of people in shaping their own development.

At this juncture, let me express gratitude to all cooperating partners, including the United Nations, who have supported our efforts and initiatives on women empowerment, helping us to end child marriages, to reduce early pregnancies, to increase school completion rates for girls, and to ensure that increasing numbers of women participate meaningfully in our nation's affairs. Madam President, humanity's progress is inseparable from global peace and security, for true stability can only be achieved when no one is left behind. Yet, we have fallen short in narrowing inequality as the gap between rich and poor nations continues to widen, and developing countries like Malawi struggle with limited fiscal space, limited technology transfer, low productivity, and limited participation in global trade. Last year, we adopted the Pact of the Future, reaffirming our collective commitment to inclusive, resilient, and sustainable global governance and development. The Republic of Malawi, therefore, calls on the international community to foster an environment that supports inclusive growth, ensuring that its benefits reach the most vulnerable. To realize this vision, we must strengthen trade and investment as engines of prosperity and harness the transformative potential of science, technology, artificial intelligence, and private sector development for national and global development. Madam President, climate change stands as the most critical existential threat of our era, with its adverse effects disproportionately impacting developing nations like Malawi. Despite contributing minimally to global greenhouse gas emissions, the Republic of Malawi endures some of the most severe consequences of climate change. The increasing frequency and intensity of severe droughts, catastrophic floods, and destructive cyclones jeopardize food security by disrupting agricultural production, displacing vulnerable communities, and threatening hard-won developmental advancements. The Republic of Malawi has lived with this reality. Erratic weather patterns threaten our agricultural backbone, pushing vulnerable communities into food insecurity and economic despair, conditions that are ripe for discord. It is therefore important that our discussion on peace must be intrinsically linked to climate resilience, sustainable agriculture, and food sovereignty. Sovereignty, just like peace, is threatened by food insecurity.

At the same time, Malawi recognizes that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence presents significant challenges, particularly for developing economies with fragile labor markets and limited technological infrastructure. Automation could disrupt employment and widen existing inequalities, while unequal access to computing capacity, data, digital infrastructure, skills, and financing risks creating a new technological divide between and within countries. Malawi, therefore, calls upon the United Nations to continue promoting an inclusive, ethical, and development-oriented global framework for AI governance. One that safeguards human dignity and employment, builds the technological capacities of developing countries, facilitates equitable access to AI technologies, and ensures that the benefits of innovation contribute directly to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. No country should be left behind in the emerging AI-driven global economy. Mr. President, In conclusion, restoring trust requires honesty, accountability, and action. Managing transformation requires courage, vision, and solidarity. The choices we make today will reverberate for generations to come. We can choose to retreat into isolationism and protectionism, or we can choose to summon the political courage required to build a fairer, more resilient, and inclusive world. Malawi stands ready to play a part. We are transforming our economy, reforming our institutions, and investing in our people. But we cannot do it alone in an unfair global environment. We stand ready to work hand in hand with all Member States to bridge the divide, restore trust in multilateralism, and give a sustainable, dignified future for all humanity. Let this First session of the General Assembly mark the turning point where the United Nations transitions from a forum of speeches to an engine of delivery. Let us build a United Nations that delivers wealth instead of poverty, resilience instead of vulnerability, and peace instead of conflict, a United Nation that truly delivers for all. Thank you very much for your attention.

In this changing environment, Mali will pursue a foreign policy based on sovereign equality of states, on diversified partnerships, on defense of national interests, and constructive engagement for peace and prosperity throughout the world. Our objective here is strategic autonomy for Mali, strategic autonomy for the Confederation of the Sahel States, the strategic autonomy for Africa in both security and development areas. And this autonomy does not mean a rupture. Rather, it seeks to make Africa into a credible and indispensable partner for global stability and prosperity. Climate change and desertification for Mali and the Sahel remain a major source of economic, social, environmental vulnerability. They affect agriculture and livelihoods. They also, we have to acknowledge it, threatening peace and security. We therefore call on member states to focus on adaptation, on access to climate finance, on indigenous technologies and solutions tailored to Sahelian realities. We advocate stronger links between efforts to combat desertification, food security initiatives, water management, conflict prevention, and resilience building. Mr. President, the world is experiencing extraordinary technological advances, including generative artificial intelligence. It is something that comes up in debate after debate. AI offers enormous opportunities, and we acknowledge that, but also significant risks. We must be lucid here. We must not simply consume AI technology. We must master it, adapt it to our realities, and contribute to its development. This requires defining and creating appropriate legal and ethical frameworks. For us, digital and technological sovereignty has become an essential dimension of national sovereignty. We must invest in skills, in research, in innovation, and infrastructure so that young people can participate fully in this transformation. For this reason, the head of state of the Republic of Mali, Assimi Goita, has established Mali's Center for Artificial Intelligence Robotics to promote our country's digital sovereignty. On the issue of international migration, Mali, which is a country of origin, transit and destination at the same time. Mali therefore reaffirms its attachment to international cooperation and considers human mobility is a benefit for humanity.

And we have advocated for full Palestinian membership in this hall. And yet, again and again, Mr. President, the collective will of this assembly has accounted the silencing effect of the veto. Malaysia will speak plainly, Mr. President. We are sick of it. Mr. President, nowhere is the need for reform more critical than in the Security Council. Nowhere are the shortcomings of the United Nations more glaring than in the Security Council. The exercise of veto must be questioned and strongly challenged by every single member of this General Assembly, particularly in cases of crimes against humanity. Resolution 76/262 has already created an accountability channel between the Council and this Assembly. We must make full use of this resolution as a launchpad for greater accountability regarding the use of veto. Expanding the Council's membership alone will not be enough to resolve its failure. It is the veto that must be challenged, and it is the veto that must be abolished. We must begin the work now. There is still time to save the global order. The paralysis of the Security Council will not be the paralysis of the United Nations. Mr. President, it is fair to say that global trust in the United Nations' ability to deliver is at an all-time low. This in turn demolishes trust in the very idea of the multilateral order. The citizens we serve and represent are afraid, Excellencies. They are watching the world order fragment. They are witnessing the reemergence of armed race. They have heard overt threat over use nuclear weapons, and they are seeing their government choose not to regulate AI and the many ways it is being abused, but instead give it more power. In such chaotic times, the only way to course correct is to rebuild trust in the power of proactive governance and multilateralism. Mr. President, trust comes from the way in which we, as the world leaders, can manage transformation forces. For centuries, Global power was concentrated in states. But today, a new source of power have emerged.

A handful of private actors now control how billions of people communicate, work, transact, and consume information. Artificial intelligence is changing how economies cooperate, how societies function, and how governments make decisions. The opportunities are enormous. but also are the risks. We must therefore ask simple question, who governs the transformation? Technology must serve humanity, never the reverse. And the answer cannot be that small number of companies or countries decide the rules for everyone else. The United Nations must continue to empower global south countries who are likely to be more greatly affected by an equitable AI development to participate in global discussion on AI. The global South cannot simply become a destination for data centers while decisions about AI are made elsewhere. We must be partners in innovation, not merely customers and market, and not merely destinations for investment. Partners involved in the decisions that will shape our future. Equitable decision making and equitable development. That means managing the enormous demands that tech infrastructure places on water, energy, land, and other resources so that the benefits of AI can be shared more broadly across the borders. Mr. President, in our hyper-connected world today, indeed, very few things stay where they begin. Technologies are rapidly shared, and they can just as rapidly disrupt. Similarly, war can also travel beyond borders. Across West Asia, escalating conflict threatens some of the world's most important routes for energy and trade, including the Strait of Hormuz, and the Bab al-Mandab. The consequences of conflict do not stop at these shores. A family in Southeast Asia has no part in these disputes, yet that family still pays the price when food, fuel, and cost of living rise. Malaysia therefore urges all parties to step back from escalation. Diplomacy has shown that dialogue is possible, that past must not be abandoned. Or we risk sending further shockwaves through global markets and needlessly bringing suffering to innocent families around the world. Mr. President, most nations in this hall are not great powers, yet Decision taken by few can shape the future for all.

challenges, such as cybersecurity, counter-terrorism and the economic disruption caused by the emergence of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and the potential for genetic engineering.

We need to bring the same constructive spirit to other areas of the global commons — AI, cybersecurity, digital technology and even outer space. We do not lack policy ideas on strengthening multilateralism, but we need commitment and action. The High-level Advisory Board on Effective Multilateralism has put forward six transformational shifts that will make the United Nations and the multilateral system future-ready. For many small States, our survival and our very success require a strong United Nations and an effective multilateral system founded on the Charter of the United Nations and international law, and complied with by all States in the world. The Forum of Small States, chaired by Singapore, will continue to work with all States, large and small, to make the United Nations stronger and ready for the future.

We will continue to contribute through platforms such as the digital pillar for the Forum of Small States and by making our governance frameworks and testing tools available to all. But the work of building trust and laying the ground for global cooperation must begin now. Ultimately, powerful engines and good brakes and common rules do not stop us or slow us down. They give us the assurance and the confidence so that we can move faster and more effectively for the benefit of all our peoples. Madam President, Excellencies, effective multilateralism requires institutions that can deliver, and that begins with a reform of the UN itself. I welcome the progress of the UN80 initiative, but reform must be strategic, not merely fiscal. Reform must strengthen the equal standing of all members. The goal is not a smaller UN for its own sake, but one that delivers better and more equitably. In this session, we will appoint the 10th Secretary-General of the UN. No one today under the age of 80 has lived in a world without the United Nations. But the UN has to earn the confidence of successive generations, and it does this through what it delivers. not what it declares on paper. The next Secretary-General must lead a UN that turns multilateral cooperation into practical results and communicates these results in an effective way to all our people. Let me at this point also pay tribute to Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. He's a good man with the courage of his convictions, and he has ably steered this organization through some very difficult years of global division. He has been a consistent voice for the Charter, for our climate and oceans, and for the rules that hold the global commons together. Finally, Madam President, effective multilateralism requires all countries to be prepared to contribute to the institutions that sustain it. For Singapore, this begins with international law. The rule of law requires institutions to give it effect. Currently, the International Court of Justice has its fullest docket in its history.

The fourth International Conference on Small Island Developing States (SIDS4), held earlier this year, marked a significant milestone for all SIDS. We welcome the adoption of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, which outlines an action plan for the next decade. Singapore will support our friends in SIDS. We launched a new technical assistance package at SIDS4, called SIDS of Change, which covers priority areas, including blue carbon. Singapore will continue to support our fellow small States, and we will share our development experience. I am happy to announce that Singapore will renew our capacity-building programme for the Forum of Small States (FOSS). We have labelled that programme FOSS for Good, a package that will offer digital-themed programmes, including Leadership and Governance in the Age of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence.

It is actually easy to understand why there is a resurgence in isolationist, protectionist and even xenophobic sentiments in the political arena all over the world. We are living in uncertain, volatile and disruptive times. The digital revolution is increasingly disrupting the way we live, work, play, communicate, organize and mobilize our societies. Non-State actors and transboundary threats, terrorism, pandemics and climate change remain a clear and present danger. Frontier issues such as artificial intelligence and cybercrime have leapt from the pages of science fiction into our daily lives. Our social cohesion is breaking down, and all too often we operate in isolated social and political bubbles.

The recent adoption of the Paris Agreement on Climate Change and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development showed that multilateralism can respond to new challenges, especially when there is political will and collective commitment. When dealing with global issues such as climate change, there is no alternative to a multilateral approach. The United Nations must also deal with emerging global

Portugal welcomes and reaffirms its support for all the priorities that Secretary-General António Guterres has pursued in his coherent, dynamic and resolute mandate, including by defending effective multilateralism, based on international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and its legal extension to new global realities, such as the oceans, combating terrorism and artificial intelligence.

Work in defense of the United Nations Charter, international law, and multilateralism. Heads of state and government, excellencies. Over the past few decades, the international order focused on promoting peace and stability has been essential to prosperity and socioeconomic progress in our societies. wars and geopolitical tensions that characterize our times have had a terrible human toll, undermining international order and consequently the chance of prosperity. That is why we must explore every opportunity for dialogue, diplomacy and peace. In the Middle East, The humanitarian tragedy must end and we must move towards the two-state solution, with Israel and Palestine coexisting as two sovereign states in peace and security. The aggressive actions by Iran and its associated armed groups must cease, including attacks on neighboring countries, merchant vessels, and civilian infrastructures. Similarly, The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz must end and freedom of navigation must be guaranteed, including safe and toll-free passage, including through the Red Sea. In Europe, we must achieve a just and lasting peace that puts an end to the brutal and illegal aggression of Russia against Ukraine. Ukraine is a partner that has the full support of Portugal and European Union. In Sudan, The most dramatic humanitarian crisis we face must come to an end. We must also remain resolute in combating the global threats of terrorism and nuclear weapons. And in the face of the new challenge posed by artificial intelligence, we must find together the right balance between innovation and regulation. One that allows us to harness its potential for the benefit of humanity, while preventing it from distorting our very essence, excellencies. The energy crisis and the rising fuel prices we are facing due to international conflicts are affecting all our peoples. Everyone is being harmed. From Asia to Europe, from Africa to the Americas, no country is immune. They have serious economic and social impact and are already having undesirable consequences for all of us and also for the parties involved. This is a senseless crisis because it's harmful to everyone.

Secondly, new issues are emerging that demand multilateral solutions in accordance with normative and cooperative arrangements. What is know called the fourth industrial revolution presents both a challenge and an opportunity. From artificial intelligence and robotization to the implementation of smart grids and 5G infrastructure and data management, to restructuring entire sectors of the economy, the impact of new technologies — on the economy, the work world and relations among States — will demand new rules of conduct at the international level. The UN must play a central role in defining them by providing compromise solutions capable of safeguard the public interest.

And today, is one of those times and therefore it's our duty to rise to the courage and the ambition present in this text in the United Nations Charter and this is why ladies and gentlemen we need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members because as the UN Charter sets out no country should be judged in its own case, no matter how powerful they are. We therefore need to strengthen all of the other main bodies and reorganise the agency's funds and programmes and provide them with more resources and more executive capacity so that they can have a more decisive impact on the great challenges that beset humanity. We must strengthen bodies like the International Criminal Court so that they can investigate, prosecute and punish those that break the rules.
